Difference and system GMM for dynamic panels

Source: R/dpnl.R
gmmpnl.Rd

The generalized method of moments estimators of a dynamic panel with unit effects: the difference estimator of Arellano and Bond (1991) and the system estimator of Arellano and Bover (1995) and Blundell and Bond (1998), with the instrument matrix built as Roodman (2009) describes it. Andreatta et al. (2023, pp. 1372-1374, table 3) fit the logged rate of waste crime in Italian provinces this way: one-step system GMM with robust errors, time effects, the lagged rate and four enforcement and organised-crime variables instrumented GMM-style by their second and third lags, the AR(1) and AR(2) tests, the Hansen test, the Hansen test of the differenced equations alone and the difference-in-Hansen test of the level instruments, with no more instruments than provinces.

Usage

gmmpnl(
  y,
  x = NULL,
  unit,
  time,
  ylag = 1,
  gmm = NULL,
  iv = NULL,
  z = NULL,
  lagmin = 2,
  lagmax = Inf,
  collapse = FALSE,
  type = "system",
  trans = "fd",
  steps = 1,
  robust = TRUE,
  wc = NULL,
  small = FALSE,
  hmat = "ab",
  cons = TRUE,
  tdum = TRUE,
  ar = 2,
  level = 0.95
)

# S3 method for class 'gmmpnl'
plot(x, ..., main = NULL, col = NULL, pal = NULL)

Arguments

y

The count of each row (a unit in a period): numbers from 0.

x

NULL or the regressors: a numeric matrix or data frame, one row per row of y; the column names name them. For plot(), a gmmpnl result.

unit

The unit of each row: labels.

time

The period of each row: numbers; each unit at most once per period.

ylag

The lags of y among the regressors: a whole number from 0 (default 1, the first-order model of Arellano and Bond 1991, eq 1).

gmm

NULL or the names of columns of x instrumented GMM-style, as the lagged outcome is.

iv

NULL (every column of x not in gmm) or the names of the columns of x that instrument themselves, IV-style; character(0) for none.

z

NULL or excluded IV-style instruments: a numeric matrix or data frame, one row per row of y.

lagmin, lagmax

The lags of the GMM-style instruments: one value, or one per GMM-style variable (the lagged outcome first); whole numbers from 1, lagmax also Inf. The defaults 2 and Inf take every lag valid for an endogenous variable (Arellano and Bond 1991, sec. 2; Roodman 2009, sec. 3.2).

collapse

TRUE for one instrument per lag rather than per lag and period (Roodman 2009, sec. 3.2); default FALSE, the full set of Arellano and Bond.

type

"system" (default, Blundell and Bond 1998; the default of Roodman's xtabond2) or "diff" (Arellano and Bond 1991).

trans

"fd" (first differences, default, Arellano and Bond 1991) or "fod" (forward orthogonal deviations, Arellano and Bover 1995).

steps

1 (default; Andreatta et al. 2023 and the default of xtabond2) or 2 (the two-step estimator).

robust

TRUE (default) for the robust one-step variance and Windmeijer's correction of the two-step variance; FALSE for the conventional one-step variance and the uncorrected two-step variance.

wc

NULL (default: as robust) or TRUE or FALSE for Windmeijer's (2005) correction of the two-step variance; it must agree with robust.

small

FALSE (default) or TRUE for the small-sample variance, t statistics and an F test as xtabond2 3.7.2 computes them (above).

hmat

"ab" (default), "dpd" or "id": H of the one-step weight, as above (Roodman 2009, secs. 3.3-3.4).

cons

TRUE (default) for a constant in the level equation of system GMM; ignored by difference GMM, which removes it.

tdum

TRUE (default) for time dummies, which Roodman (2009, sec. 3.3) advises so that the errors are not correlated across units.

ar

The highest order of the Arellano-Bond tests: a whole number from 0 (default 2, as xtabond2).

level

The confidence level of the intervals.

...

Passed to the base-graphics call.

main

NULL (a default title) or one string.

col

NULL (the palette) or colours.

pal

NULL (the session palette, see plotopt()) or a palette name for blpal().

Value

An object of class gmmpnl, a list: coef (term, est, se, z (t with small), p, lo, hi); tests (test, stat, df, p: AR(1) to AR(ar), Sargan, Hansen and, for system GMM, the Hansen test without the level GMM-style instruments and the difference-in-Hansen test, or their Sargan counterparts with the conventional one-step variance); wald, one row (test, "Wald" or "F", stat, df1, df2, p); xwald, the same as xtabond2 prints it (over every coefficient); resid, y - x b in levels, one per row of y; fit, one row: n (the rows of the transformed equation for difference GMM, of the levels for system GMM, as xtabond2 counts), groups, inst, omin, oavg, omax (rows per group), steps, k and sigma2; vcov; inst, the instruments' names; dropped, the time dummies dropped; dummies, those kept; note; type; trans; robust; small; and level.

Details

The model is y_it = a_1 y_i,t-1 + ... + a_L y_i,t-L + x_it b + d_t + u_i + v_it with L = ylag. Periods are the distinct values of time in order: lags count positions in that order, and a unit without a row in a period has a gap there. A row enters the levels when the unit has the ylag periods before it; the transformed equation is the first difference of two such rows in consecutive periods (trans = "fd"), or the forward orthogonal deviation of a row from the mean of the unit's later rows, scaled by sqrt(T / (T + 1)) and dated one period later (trans = "fod", Arellano and Bover 1995, sec. 3; Roodman 2009, eq 21), which loses no more than the last row of a unit with gaps.

GMM-style instruments (Roodman 2009, sec. 3.2) are made for the lagged outcome (when ylag > 0, first) and for the columns of x named in gmm: for the transformed equation dated t, the levels of the variable at t - l for l from lagmin to lagmax, zero where the unit has no row, one column per period and lag, or one per lag with collapse = TRUE. For the level equation of system GMM, the difference at t - lagmin + 1 (one column per period, or one); the other lags are redundant (Roodman 2009, sec. 3.4). Lags count from the variable: the default lagmin = 2 takes y_i,t-2 and earlier for the equation in t, the standard choice for an endogenous variable, and lagmin = 1 treats a column as predetermined. IV-style instruments (one column each, transformed in the transformed equation and in levels in the level equation, Roodman 2009, eq 24) are the columns of x in iv, the columns of z, the time dummies and, in system GMM, the constant (which is in the level equation only). Columns of instruments that are zero throughout are dropped; time dummies collinear with the other regressors in the stacked equations are dropped, and named in dropped.

The one-step weight is (sum_i Z_i' H_i Z_i)^-1. With hmat = "ab" (the default), H_i is what the errors' variance would be with independent, homoskedastic idiosyncratic errors and no unit effects in the level equation: M M' for the transformed rows (2 on the diagonal and -1 next to it for differences, the identity for deviations), M between transformed and level rows and the identity for the levels (Roodman 2009, eqs 22-23 and 26); "dpd" zeroes the blocks between the equations, and "id" takes the identity throughout, as Blundell and Bond (1998) did. The two-step weight is the inverse of sum_i Z_i' e_i e_i' Z_i with the one-step residuals. A singular weight matrix is replaced by its Moore-Penrose inverse, and the result says so. With robust = TRUE (the default) the one-step variance is the robust sandwich (Roodman 2009, eq 15) and the two-step variance is corrected as Windmeijer (2005) shows (Roodman 2009, eq 18); with robust = FALSE the one-step variance is the conventional s2 (X'Z A Z'X)^-1, eq 14 with Var(z e) = s2 Z'HZ, A = (Z'HZ)^-1 and s2 as for Sargan's statistic below, and the two-step variance is the uncorrected (X'Z A_2 Z'X)^-1 (Roodman 2009, p. 96). wc is the older name of the two-step choice: left NULL it follows robust, and a value that contradicts robust, or wc with one step, is refused.

Roodman (2009, p. 123) describes small of xtabond2 only as "small-sample corrections to the covariance matrix estimate, resulting in t-test instead of z-test statistics for the coefficients and an F test instead of a Wald chi2 test for overall fit"; small = TRUE makes the corrections as xtabond2 3.7.2 computes them. With n the rows of the equation reported (fit$n), w the rows of the transformed equation in system GMM with hmat other than "id" and n otherwise, G the groups, k the coefficients and c 1 for the constant of system GMM (0 otherwise): the conventional one-step variance is multiplied by w / (w - k), and the robust one-step variance and both two-step variances by (n - 1) / (n - k) * G / (G - 1); sigma2 is multiplied by w / (w - k). The coefficients have t statistics on df_r degrees of freedom and the joint test is F = W / q on q and df_r, with df_r = n - q - c for the conventional one-step variance and G - c otherwise. The Sargan and Hansen statistics are unchanged; so are the Arellano-Bond statistics, except after the conventional one-step variance, where the program scales sigma2 in the errors' variance by w / (w - k) and leaves the coefficients' variance in the statistic unscaled, and so does this function. Roodman's program also lets the variance be clustered on other variables, which multiplies each cluster's terms of the moments' variance by G / (G - 1) and drops that factor from the variance; this function clusters by unit only.

wald is the joint test that the coefficients other than the constant are 0, W = b' V^-1 b over them, on q degrees of freedom counted as xtabond2 3.7.2 counts them, with or without small: the rank of the regressors in the levels (system GMM; the transformed equation is left out of the test) or in the transformed equation, less c; without a constant, one less again when the vector of ones i lies in their column space, which the program finds when i'X_p (X'X)^-1 X_p'i, X_p those rows and X the whole stack, is within the machine epsilon times the groups times the periods of the rows of X_p, relatively. The program's own statistic takes b' V^-1 b over every coefficient, the constant's included, while counting q without it; this function leaves the constant out of the statistic too, so that the two agree when no constant is estimated. xwald is the program's statistic, b' V^-1 b over every coefficient on the same q (and F = W / q with small), so that its printed line can be reproduced; print() shows it on a second line when it differs from wald.

Two values differ from the program's by design. sigma2 is that of the one-step residuals, which Sargan's statistic uses, also with steps = 2, where xtabond2 reports the two-step residuals' value. With the conventional one-step variance the Arellano-Bond statistics take the error variance as s2 times the covariances of independent errors through the differences whatever hmat (Roodman 2009, n. 19), where with hmat = "id" in system GMM the program takes sigma2 from the levels and H = I there; the identity is the weight of Blundell and Bond's first step, not the covariance of differenced errors.

resid holds y - x b in levels for every row of the level equation (NA for rows without the ylag periods before), the unit effects included; Andreatta et al. (2023, p. 1376) pass such residuals of the dynamic model to Pesaran's test of cross-sectional dependence (pcdtst()) and to Moran's I for each year (gmoran()).

Andreatta et al. (2023), step by step. Their table 3 is one-step system GMM with robust errors "with small-sample adjustments" (note): type = "system", steps = 1, robust = TRUE, small = TRUE; time effects, tdum = TRUE; the lagged rate, ylag = 1, and the four enforcement and organised-crime variables in gmm, instrumented by "their second and third lags" (p. 1373), lagmin = 2, lagmax = 3, or by "Lag 2 and earlier lags" (table note), lagmax = Inf, the other drivers IV-style (iv); the difference of lag 1 in the level equation is what lagmin = 2 gives there. Their tests are the rows of tests: AR(1) and AR(2), Hansen, "Hansen-level", the Hansen test of the first-differenced model ("Hansen without level GMM"), and "Hansen-diff" ("Difference-in-Hansen"); "No. of instruments" is fit$inst, kept below the 102 provinces (note warns otherwise). The supplementary "standard" model with first lags as instruments is lagmin = 1 for the variables taken as predetermined. Before choosing a dynamic model they ran Wooldridge's test on the static model's residuals (wsctst(), n. 9, F(1, 101)), and they compare the coefficient of the lagged rate with pooled least squares (lm()) and fixed effects (fepnl() with the lag among the regressors). Their checks of spatial dependence are gmoran() and gearc() on the rate with several weight matrices, pcdtst() on the residuals of the static and dynamic models and gmoran() on each year's residuals (p. 1376); their structural breaks (2013, 2014, 2015) are step dummies among the IV-style columns of x, and their principal components of the enforcement rates are stats::prcomp().

Demir and Ozcan (2023, table 4) fit system GMM to 37 OECD countries over 2003-2017: the log rate of persons held in prison on its lag, the log forest area per person and the log CO2 emissions per head, with the controls the tests found endogenous instrumented GMM-style; where AR(2) rejected, "the instruments were used at least with their third lags" (lagmin = 3, with ar = 3), and the instruments were kept no more than the countries (collapse, lagmax; note warns otherwise), with the Hansen test above 0.10.

The Arellano-Bond statistics (Arellano and Bond 1991, eqs 8-9) are those of serial correlation of orders 1 to ar in the differenced residuals of the estimate reported, also after deviations, with the variance's terms taken from that estimate's residuals, weight and variance (Roodman 2009, sec. 3.5), and with the error variance taken as s2 H for the conventional one-step variance (Roodman 2009, n. 19, the covariances of independent homoskedastic errors through the transformation and the differences, whatever hmat); AR(2) is the one that tests the instruments. Hansen's statistic is that of the two-step estimate, whichever step is reported, as robust overidentification tests need (Roodman 2009, sec. 2.5); Sargan's is that of the one-step residuals, e'Z (Z'HZ)^-1 Z'e / s2 with s2 the sum of the squared one-step residuals of the transformed equation over the sum of their diagonal elements of H (this function's estimate of the variance; Arellano and Bond 1991, p. 282, write the statistic with an estimate of it). In system GMM the Hansen test without the GMM-style instruments of the level equation re-estimates the model with the rest, weighted by the corresponding block of the full two-step moment variance (Roodman 2009, n. 24), and the difference-in-Hansen statistic is the full statistic less that one, on as many degrees of freedom as there are instruments left out. With the conventional one-step variance Sargan's statistic is the one reported for the instruments, and the difference test is the difference-in-Sargan, the model re-estimated with the block of Z'HZ (Roodman 2009, n. 24). wald is the joint test of the coefficients other than the constant (above). Every test is on m - k degrees of freedom or fewer, m the instruments and k the coefficients. When the instruments outnumber the groups, note says so (Roodman 2009, sec. 2.6). Inference is normal unless small = TRUE. Andreatta et al. describe their instruments both as "their second and third lags" (p. 1373) and as "Lag 2 and earlier lags" (table 3, note); lagmin and lagmax take either reading.

The plot draws the coefficients other than the constant and the time dummies, with their intervals, and returns what it drew.

References

Arellano, M. and Bond, S. (1991). Some tests of specification for panel data: Monte Carlo evidence and an application to employment equations. The Review of Economic Studies, 58(2), 277-297. doi:10.2307/2297968

Arellano, M. and Bover, O. (1995). Another look at the instrumental variable estimation of error-components models. Journal of Econometrics, 68(1), 29-51. doi:10.1016/0304-4076(94)01642-D

Blundell, R. and Bond, S. (1998). Initial conditions and moment restrictions in dynamic panel data models. Journal of Econometrics, 87(1), 115-143. doi:10.1016/S0304-4076(98)00009-8

Windmeijer, F. (2005). A finite sample correction for the variance of linear efficient two-step GMM estimators. Journal of Econometrics, 126(1), 25-51. doi:10.1016/j.jeconom.2004.02.005

Roodman, D. (2009). How to do xtabond2: an introduction to difference and system GMM in Stata. The Stata Journal, 9(1), 86-136. doi:10.1177/1536867X0900900106

Andreatta, D., Favarin, S., Lisciandra, M. and Millemaci, E. (2023). Digging into waste: an analysis of waste crime in the Italian provinces. Regional Studies, 57(7), 1367-1379. doi:10.1080/00343404.2022.2135697

Demir, C. and Ozcan, S. E. (2023). Do air quality and green space reduce propensity to crime?: an empirical investigation of OECD countries. Management of Environmental Quality: An International Journal, 34(2), 351-367. doi:10.1108/MEQ-08-2022-0235

Examples

# 60 provinces over 8 years: a logged rate with persistence 0.5 and one
# endogenous driver, simulated
set.seed(7)
d <- expand.grid(year = 2010:2017, prov = paste0("p", 1:60))
u <- rnorm(60)[as.integer(substring(d$prov, 2))]
d$enf <- u + rnorm(480)
d$y <- 0
for (i in which(d$year > 2010)) {
  d$y[i] <- 0.5 * d$y[i - 1] + 0.3 * d$enf[i] + u[i] + rnorm(1)
}
r <- gmmpnl(d$y, d["enf"], d$prov, d$year, gmm = "enf", lagmax = 3,
            collapse = TRUE)
r
#> gmmpnl: system GMM (fd), step 1, 420 rows, 60 groups, 13 instruments
#> robust variance
#>     term         est         se           z            p         lo        hi
#>     L1.y  0.63565326 0.06952086  9.14334550 6.054957e-20  0.4993949 0.7719116
#>      enf  0.92497344 0.19159312  4.82780094 1.380490e-06  0.5494578 1.3004891
#>  (const) -0.06954309 0.13468780 -0.51632809 6.056253e-01 -0.3335263 0.1944401
#>    t2011  0.26161153 0.23231848  1.12609006 2.601274e-01 -0.1937243 0.7169474
#>    t2012 -0.01923081 0.19584762 -0.09819271 9.217793e-01 -0.4030851 0.3646235
#>    t2013 -0.03271092 0.19746408 -0.16565506 8.684284e-01 -0.4197334 0.3543116
#>    t2014  0.19530957 0.21204614  0.92107109 3.570133e-01 -0.2202932 0.6109124
#>    t2015  0.04273779 0.21878075  0.19534529 8.451226e-01 -0.3860646 0.4715402
#>    t2016  0.08698987 0.18530371  0.46944485 6.387517e-01 -0.2761987 0.4501785
#> Wald chi2(8) = 1275.2, p 5.394e-270
#> Wald chi2(8) = 1560.9, p 0 (every coefficient, as xtabond2 prints it)
#>                      test       stat df            p
#>                     AR(1) -5.0629586 NA 4.127995e-07
#>                     AR(2)  0.6919913 NA 4.889428e-01
#>                    Sargan  8.8777291  4 6.422940e-02
#>                    Hansen  9.3189947  4 5.360236e-02
#>  Hansen without level GMM  0.6621633  2 7.181465e-01
#>      Difference-in-Hansen  8.6568314  2 1.318843e-02
r$tests
#>                       test       stat df            p
#> 1                    AR(1) -5.0629586 NA 4.127995e-07
#> 2                    AR(2)  0.6919913 NA 4.889428e-01
#> 3                   Sargan  8.8777291  4 6.422940e-02
#> 4                   Hansen  9.3189947  4 5.360236e-02
#> 5 Hansen without level GMM  0.6621633  2 7.181465e-01
#> 6     Difference-in-Hansen  8.6568314  2 1.318843e-02

# the specification of Andreatta et al. (2023, table 3) on simulated
# data: the lagged rate and four drivers GMM-style by their second and
# third lags, collapsed so that the instruments stay below the
# provinces, two exogenous drivers, time effects, one-step robust
# errors with small-sample adjustments
set.seed(23)
np <- 102
d <- expand.grid(year = 2010:2019, prov = paste0("p", 1:np))
u <- rnorm(np)[as.integer(substring(d$prov, 2))]
n <- nrow(d)
for (v in c("clear", "conv", "mafia", "assoc")) d[[v]] <- u + rnorm(n)
d$gdp <- rnorm(n)
d$recyc <- rnorm(n)
d$wcrim <- 0
for (i in which(d$year > 2010)) {
  d$wcrim[i] <- 0.4 * d$wcrim[i - 1] - 0.1 * d$clear[i] +
    0.2 * d$mafia[i] + 0.1 * d$gdp[i] + u[i] + rnorm(1)
}
en <- c("clear", "conv", "mafia", "assoc")
a <- gmmpnl(d$wcrim, d[c(en, "gdp", "recyc")], d$prov, d$year, gmm = en,
            lagmin = 2, lagmax = 3, collapse = TRUE, small = TRUE)
a$tests
#>                       test      stat df            p
#> 1                    AR(1) -4.694829 NA 0.0000026683
#> 2                    AR(2)  1.432563 NA 0.1519828001
#> 3                   Sargan  9.750661 10 0.4626343573
#> 4                   Hansen 11.268943 10 0.3369524384
#> 5 Hansen without level GMM  1.868157  5 0.8670707506
#> 6     Difference-in-Hansen  9.400786  5 0.0941069902
a$fit$inst < a$fit$groups
#> [1] TRUE
# the static model's serial correlation and the dynamic residuals'
# cross-sectional dependence
wsctst(d$wcrim, d[c(en, "gdp", "recyc")], d$prov, d$year)
#> wsctst: Wooldridge test of serial correlation, F(1, 101) = 73.206, p 1.336e-13
#> lagged residual -0.2747 (se 0.02634; -0.5 without correlation), 816 pairs
k <- !is.na(a$resid)
pcdtst(a$resid[k], d$prov[k], d$year[k])
#>            cd             p           rho        absrho         pairs 
#> -2.063590e+00  3.905661e-02 -9.584211e-03  2.965807e-01  5.151000e+03 
#>         units       periods 
#>  1.020000e+02  9.000000e+00
